rv.q: I have no doubt that it marks the decisive emergence of a distinctive voice in American theater.
Not the imaginative way playwright Lydia R. Diamond tells it in "Smart People," a sexy, serious and very, very funny modern-day comedy of manners.
The playwright more than satisfies that promise with a quick-thinking, fast-talking look at four, yes, smart — not to mention good looking — Harvard people.
The result is both a provocative dialectic and a lively comedy, with prickly characters that push back against one another's preconceptions, often questioning their own in the process.
Although Ms. Diamond is clearly herself a powerfully smart writer, you come away from “Smart People” feeling like you’ve attended a marathon series of seminars, not a persuasively drawn drama.
Although Diamond raises resonant questions, much of her spitballing hits right on the nose.
The result feels less like a play than a PowerPoint presentation.
It’s a case of smart people, dumb dramaturgy.
Smart People is not just a “smart” play but a wise one.
Smart People is very funny because it reflects a very sympathetic human foible; the desire resolve our racial conflicts without messing things up every time we open our mouths.
There is much to ponder here and it is awfully dense, but if you're up for it, I do recommend "Smart People."
Smart People provides such thought-provoking entertainment that it's too bad to report that at times it seems like a series of conversations in search of a play.
Smart People, however, is a clever, perceptive look at race in the work place and how it impinges on romantic relations in our private lives.
"Smart People," which opened Thursday night at the Second Stage Theatre, is a patchwork quilt of a play, a mélange of scenes about race in America without a distinctive through-pattern.

Besides the characters venting ongoing frustrations about their careers and getting into meandering discussions on the presence of racism, no overall storyline develops and very little occurs for two hours and 15 minutes.
“Confrontational People” would be a more apt title.
But for every scene that comes alive with humor, there are two that turn didactic.
Diamond has given these fine actors little to work with in terms of depth. Kenny Leon�s direction does nothing to elevate or simplify the evening.
With unfocused plot development and language that dances around its point, Smart People feels like a rough draft of a potentially greater play.
But it’s much less smart, and far more muddled, than the author probably intended.
In short, all four actors are brilliant, edgy and captivating in their respective roles.
In the hands of an enormously talented cast, Smart People shines.
Still, I was finding the well-written Smart People, directed by Tony winner Kenny Leon (A Raisin in the Sun, Holler If Ya Hear Me), to be a little trite.
The play itself, though, barely passes.
Yet the play fails to completely engage the audience for a couple of reasons: first, the characters are so self-involved and self-important that they become blatantly unlikeable.
It feels like a construct framed so a lecture and a theory can be debated and presented to us.
Do yourself a favor and skip Smart People.
